articles.title: A Chicago family replaced a tiny patch of backyard grass with model railway tracks in the late 1990s; more than 20 years later, the miniature village fills the entire yard and can run seven trains at once
articles.summary: What started as a small family hobby has gradually turned an ordinary Chicago backyard into a miniature railway town.
articles.body: What started as a small family hobby has gradually turned an ordinary Chicago backyard into a miniature railway town. The Rustemeyer family in Norwood Park has spent more than two decades building an elaborate garden railroad, transforming a modest patch of grass into a landscape filled with train tracks, tiny buildings, flowers and carefully arranged details. According to Block Club Chicago and WBBM Newsradio, which visited the family home in October 2026, the railway now covers virtually the entire backyard and can accommodate seven trains running at the same time. What makes the project particularly special is that it has grown into a shared family tradition, bringing together generations through a common love of model trains. Scroll down to read more.A hobby that began with one small stretch of grassThe idea came from Judy's father, William Rustemeyer, who had been interested in model trains for years and initially maintained a railway layout in the family's basement. Towards the end of the 1990s, he decided to take his hobby outdoors and create something that could become part of the backyard.The family initially set aside a small oval-shaped section of grass in the middle of the garden for the tracks. What seemed like a relatively modest addition soon became an annual project, with new sections added as the family found more ways to develop the layout.Not everyone was immediately convinced. Shirley, who had spent years looking after her garden, was initially hesitant about giving up the green space. However, she eventually became an active part of the project, helping Judy incorporate flowers and other decorative elements into the railway. Today, the family calls the garden the Norwood Junction 5R Railroad. articles.title: AP Exclusive: Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although they did not specify when that would be carried out. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

A legal group representing Iranians held by Immigration and Customs Enforcement said at least a dozen Iranian detainees had been notified over the past week that they were being deported to Iran, with some told it could be as soon as this coming Sunday. The legal group, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, brought the lawsuit in which the new court documents were released.

Earlier court filings and emails show the administration held talks with Iran on deportations that took place last year and shortly before the war. But the revelation that it was maintaining those contacts even after the war broke out highlighted the administration's resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees.

"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.

"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."

"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal." Georgiev-Remmel told the court there was no specific date set to carry out any removals.

The court documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iran during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."

The State Department said it generally does not comment on pending litigation or private diplomatic discussions. It referred other questions to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lawsuit has been challenging deportations of Iranian asylum seekers

The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund said Thursday the Iranian detainees were contacted by the Iranian Interest Section, an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs, in the past week and notified of an upcoming deportation flight to Iran through Pakistan. Some had also been notified by DHS officials of the upcoming deportation.

One of those detainees attempted suicide once he learned he might be returned to Iran, according to Yasmine Chubin, the executive director of the organization. He was one of two people who were subsequently moved across state lines to a detention center where detainees are often sent immediately before a removal.

None of the detainees who have been contacted have been provided any information in writing from immigration authorities, the legal group said.

"Some of those same asylum applicants, and others who could face the same death, are being sent back — all against a backdrop of further and intensifying U.S. bombing of Iran," Chubin said. "This flight must be stopped."

Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.

The lawsuit on the Iranian asylum seekers alleges the Trump administration's immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings state.

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in ICE custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government. The judge overseeing the case said it was possible the government shared the confidential information, but appeared skeptical of claims that have arisen in the lawsuit that DHS has a coordinated policy of sharing those records.

In addition, hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

Deportations of Iranians have been historically rare

During the Oct. 15 hearing, Reyes warned government attorneys that she would initiate contempt proceedings if the administration violated her order to give the court advance notice of any planned deportation flights.

"We are talking about sending individuals in our care and custody to a country that we have bombed and we may continue bombing, and is a declared enemy of this country," Reyes said.

In a court filing Wednesday, the Justice Department said the judge's order effectively served as an injunction against the government "given the possibility of sanctions and contempt dangling overhead."

Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran.

But under the Trump administration, which is carrying out a broad immigration crackdown, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations.

Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country, but it has also meant deporting people to other countries they have no connection with.

The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won't take their people back. During Trump's second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S.

In June, an Iranian woman was among two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic.

Riddle reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press reporter Matthew Lee contributed to this report. Follow the AP's coverage of the Iran war at .

articles.title: Henry Nowak's killer has sentence increased to 25 years
articles.summary: Judges ruled Vickrum Digwa's original term was unduly lenient and refused his bid to have it cut.
articles.body:
A man jailed for life for murdering Henry Nowak has had his minimum prison term increased to 25 years by the Court of Appeal.

Vickrum Digwa was serving a minimum of 21 years for stabbing 18-year-old student Nowak with a large dagger in Belmont Road, Southampton, on 3 December 2025.

The Attorney General referred the case to the Court of Appeal on the grounds it was "unduly lenient", while Digwa also challenged his jail term as "manifestly excessive".

The Lady Chief Justice quashed the sentence, ruling the original term "did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder".

Digwa, who was also refused permission to appeal, told police Henry had attacked and racially abused him, which led to Henry, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, being handcuffed as he lay dying.

The trial judge later found Digwa's accusations of racism to be a lie. Then 22, he was jailed for life at Southampton Crown Court in June.

Both appeals were heard on Thursday by Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr, Mr Justice Nicklin and Mr Justice Wall, with Digwa appearing via video link from HMP Frankland.

The Lady Chief Justice said the trial judge had been entitled to start at 15 years, as he found Digwa had not taken the knife to the scene intending to commit a crime.

But she said a "very significant uplift" was needed because of the use of the large kirpan.

A kirpan is a religious knife which baptised Sikhs are expected to carry at all times, and the law allows it to be carried in public for religious reasons.

Digwa wore a small kirpan around his neck, but was also carrying a larger one on a belt, in keeping with an order of Sikhs known as the Nihang.

The fact that initially carrying the knife may have been lawful "does not reduce the seriousness of its subsequent lethal use", she said.

She said the original sentence had understated the repeated use of a large dagger with intent to kill, and the "deliberate cruelty, additional suffering and obstruction" that followed.

"It was not only lenient, but unduly so," she said.

With time spent on remand deducted, Digwa must serve at least 24 years and 190 days before he can be considered for parole.

In a statement, Henry's family called the decision "an important step towards justice" but said "no sentence, however long, can ever give Henry his life back".

They continued: "We have been given a life sentence of grief. There is no appeal for us, no reduction in our suffering and no prospect of ever getting our son back."

They said their "fight for justice is far from over" and that they would support an independent rapid review being carried out by Alex Chalk.

Attorney General Ellie Reeves said: "The brutality and cruelty of this case horrified me, and I know that feeling is shared by the British public.

"My thoughts remain with Henry's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

"No sentence can ever fill the void left by his loss, and I hope this outcome goes some way towards bringing them the justice they deserve."

During the hearing, Jonathan Polnay KC, for the Attorney General, argued the 21-year term did not sufficiently reflect "the very high degree of seriousness of the offending".

He said Digwa had abused the legal exemption allowing Sikhs to carry religious blades, which permitted him to have the dagger, and that this was "on at least one level analogous to an abuse of trust".

Imran Khan KC, defending, argued the trial judge had counted overlapping aggravating factors more than once.

"To put it pithily, the Attorney General says 21 years was too little. We say it was too much," he said.

The judges agreed some factors should not have counted against Digwa, including the community impact of the case, which he had not anticipated or intended.

Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, was jailed for three years in July for assisting an offender by removing the knife from the scene. She abandoned an appeal against her sentence shortly before Thursday's hearing.

Digwa has also applied to appeal against his murder conviction, which will be decided separately.

articles.title: Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch
articles.summary: Democrats have taken control of the House and Senate, and are eyeing some more with several key races still too close to call.
articles.body:
Democrats have been celebrating their sweeping midterm victories, including flipping control of both chambers of Congress - but several critical races were still too close to be called on Thursday.

Votes are still being counted in two surprisingly tight Senate races in historically red states, Alaska and Mississippi, which could decide the true scale of Democrats' majority.

Several US House races are also too close to call, including that of Lauren Boebert, a prominent ally of President Donald Trump, who is facing a tight re-election contest in Colorado against Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.

Here are the races Americans are watching closely.

What and who are on the ballot: The race for Mississippi's Senate seat remains dramatically close with Democrat Scott Colom leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by a little over 1,100 votes. The state has until 10 November to count provisional and late-arriving mail ballots.

On the campaign trail, Colom focused his message on plans to address economic concerns, while Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was endorsed by Trump and campaigned with him.

Why it matters: If Colom wins, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875 - and the first Democrat since 1982. Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and showed up in large numbers this election.

What and who are on the ballot: It's another extremely tight race being watched nationally with Democrat Mary Peltola leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes with more ballots to be counted.

Peltola, a former congresswoman and Native American, campaigned for "fish, family and freedom", while two-term Republican Senator Sullivan focused on his efforts to get Americans tax cuts and "unleash Alaska's energy potential".

Why it matters: The race has been marred with controversy because of the appearance of another candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.

Last week, The New York Times reported allegations that Peltola and Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting the independent Dan Sullivan in order to siphon votes from the Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola has denied any knowledge of such a scheme.

3. A number of House races in purple and red states

What and who are on the ballot: Trump ally Lauren Boebert is trailing Democrat Eileen Laubacher by a narrow margin in Colorado 's Fourth District with 7% of votes left to be counted. In Tennessee 's reliably Republican Fourth District, Representative Scott DesJarlais is trailing Democrat Victoria Broderick. In Arizona 's Second District, incumbent Republican Eli Crane is leading Democrat Jonathan Nez by fewer than 4,000 votes with still many to be counted.

Why it matters: A loss for Boebert, DesJarlais and other Republicans in House races in Nevada and Ohio would mean an even larger majority for Democrats in the chamber - and a bigger rejection of Trump and his Make America Great Again movement.

What and who are on the ballot: California Proposition 40 would require a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's roughly 200 billionaires to raise tens of billions of dollars in revenue. As of Wednesday, a million more people had voted against the measure than in favour, though only 61% of votes have been counted.

Why it matters: The measure would mark the first-ever wealth tax on billionaires in the US, which proponents say would raise $100bn for health care and education. But the proposition divided Democrats, with Governor Gavin Newsom opposing it.

What and who are on the ballot: For Kansas's next governor, Democrat Cindy Holscher is leading Republican Ty Masterson by a few thousand votes.

Holscher campaigned over escalating prices, while Masterson touted his pro-business, pro-agriculture, and pro-oil and gas credentials.

Why it matters: For more than 50 years, Kansas has elected governors from the opposite party of their predecessors. If Masterson wins, that trend would continue. Holscher's victory would break it by putting another Democrat in office after two-term Governor Laura Kelly.

articles.title: Eight killed in series of shootings in western Turkey
articles.summary: Victims are found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
articles.body:
Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.

The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.

The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in Eskişehir province.

CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.

Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.

Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.

Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.

The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.

In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

articles.title: Sound of Music star Christopher Plummer's widow donated 8 acres from their 40-year-old property; another 8 acres were bought to help create a 750-acre nature preserve
articles.summary: Christopher Plummer’s widow, Elaine Taylor, has donated eight acres of land cherished by the couple for four decades to help establish a 750-acre nature
articles.body: Christopher Plummer’s widow, Elaine Taylor, has donated eight acres of land cherished by the couple for four decades to help establish a 750-acre nature preserve in Connecticut. The donation, alongside the purchase of another eight acres from the late actor’s estate, has helped Aspetuck Land Trust protect a significant stretch of land along the Weston-Wilton border. The property, once a familiar setting for the couple’s walks with their dogs, is now part of a wider conservation effort intended to preserve open landscapes and create a connected forest reserve for future generations.Christopher Plummer’s widow donates land for a 750-acre nature preserveAccording to Aspetuck Land Trust, Taylor donated eight acres of the property she shared with Plummer to the conservation organisation. The parcel lies in Wilton, directly across the road from her home in Weston, and has long been associated with the couple’s everyday life.The land was particularly meaningful to Taylor and Plummer, who spent around 40 years enjoying the property. Their regular walks included a loop through the fields with their 4 dogs, a routine Taylor recalled when discussing the donation with CTInsider.The couple would walk down to the fields and return along the same route, sometimes completing the loop more than once. Taylor described the land as having been part of their lives for four decades, making its preservation a personal decision as well as a contribution to the wider community.Plummer, who died in 2021, became internationally recognised for playing Captain Georg von Trapp in the 1965 film The Sound of Music. His career also included an Academy Award-winning performance in Beginners, for which he received the best supporting actor Oscar in 2012 at the age of 82.The donation was accompanied by a separate purchase of another eight acres from Plummer’s estate, bringing the total land protected through the transaction to approximately 16 acres.CTInsider reported that the donated portion was valued at around $900,000. The land trust purchased the additional parcel through what its executive director, David Brant, described as a bargain sale.Although the purchased property was valued at approximately $1.78 million, Aspetuck Land Trust acquired it for roughly $900,000. Combined with Taylor’s donation, the transaction enabled the organisation to protect a substantial piece of land without paying its full market value.The property includes open fields and traditional stone walls, features that distinguish it from woodland areas made up almost entirely of trees. Brant described the acquisition as particularly important because it would help connect other protected parcels into a much larger natural landscape.A larger forest reserve takes shape along the Weston-Wilton borderThe Plummer property forms part of Aspetuck Land Trust’s long-running effort to assemble a 750-acre nature preserve along the Weston-Wilton border.The organisation has been working to connect individual properties into a continuous landscape rather than protecting isolated pieces of land. According to its Weston Wilton Forest Reserve information, the project is intended to safeguard one of the region’s remaining unfragmented forests.Aspetuck Land Trust has protected 255 acres so far that connect with several other conservation properties, helping build the larger 750-acre forest corridor. Since 2017, it has successfully protected 169 acres through support from its members and funding from Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.The effort forms part of a broader regional conservation strategy. Aspetuck Land Trust explained that the Weston-Wilton forest initiative was connected to a wider Green Corridor planned across Weston, Easton, Fairfield and Westport.The organisation was also working alongside Wilton Land Conservation Trust to protect areas of natural habitat threatened by development and the fragmentation of forests.What will visitors find at the newly opened preserveThe Plummer property has also become part of a growing public recreational resource. Aspetuck Land Trust described the Weston Wilton Forest Reserve as a newly opened 750-acre interior forest, highlighting the Plummer property as one of its latest additions. articles.title: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
articles.summary: California has historically had the largest population of people on death row in the US.
articles.body:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.

"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.

The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.

The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.

Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.

Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".

California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.

Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".

He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.

Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.

He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".

"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.

"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."

Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.

Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.

He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".

"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.

Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.

At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.

It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.

Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row .

Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.

"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.

Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.

"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."

Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.

"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.

On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.

While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.

No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.

California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.

But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

articles.title: Over 1,000 tonnes of sewage seen at Doncaster landfill site
articles.summary: The Environment Agency says it has issued the operator with a series of actions after an inspection.
articles.body:
More than 1,000 tonnes of "sewage sludge" have been seen at a landfill site near Doncaster, according to an MP for the town.

Lee Pitcher said in a Facebook post he had been told the waste was being stored in "an uncovered stockpile" at the site in Finningley.

The Labour MP said he had been in contact with the Environment Agency (EA), which confirmed on Thursday that it had "set out a series of actions" for the site's operator following an inspection.

The landfill, located in a former quarry, is operated by Tetron Finningley Ltd, which has not previously responded when contacted for comment by the BBC.

Pitcher, who is the MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, said EA officers visited the landfill on 9 October and, after he "chased" them for their findings, they responded on Tuesday.

He said the EA had told him that during the visit "approximately 1,000 tonnes of sewage sludge were observed being stored externally in an uncovered stockpile" and had "identified concerns regarding whether site activities were being undertaken in accordance with the operating techniques and management arrangements described within the approved documents".

Pitcher said the EA had given the landfill operator until 10 November to resolve the issue.

The MP said he had subsequently contacted the EA again about "potential asbestos disposal at the site, along with the air quality and environmental ramifications this could bring".

He said he was concerned that the business may no longer be viable if it continues to remain closed.

In a statement on Facebook, he said: "For months, we have raised concerns about the terrible odours coming from the neighbouring site, the effects on our staff and customers, and our inability to operate safely.

"Despite those reports, the situation has continued.

"Unfortunately, while the authorities have been investigating, the financial consequences for Doncaster Moto Parc have been devastating.

"We are now facing the very real possibility of losing the business altogether."

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: "We expect site operators to manage odour effectively and have identified issues around odour management at this site.

"Following an inspection, we have set out a series of actions that we expect the operator to comply with and will not hesitate to take further enforcement action should that be required."

articles.title: Second batch of Mandelson papers set to be published before Christmas
articles.summary: Documents were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a police investigation.
articles.body:
The government is preparing to publish more documents about the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador.

Batches of papers were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a Metropolitan Police investigation.

The Cabinet Office has now said a number of extra documents will be published, likely before Christmas. Some will still be withheld at the request of the Met.

Cat Little, permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office, said that some of the documents could "now be published without prejudicing their investigation".

The Met Police had launched an investigation over allegations that, while he was serving as a government minister, Lord Mandelson had passed on market-sensitive government information to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Writing to the chair of Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, Little said: "The Cabinet Office is now beginning the process to prepare these documents so that they may be laid before the House in response to the humble address motion as soon as possible."

She said the documents would be reviewed and in some instances may need to be redacted "for the purposes of avoiding prejudice to national security or international relations".

The process is expected to be completed before Parliament rises for the Christmas recess on 17 December.

Lord Mandelson was arrested on 23 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

He has repeatedly let it be known that he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

"Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing," the Met Police said in a statement.

The lifelong Labour politician became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025, but was sacked in September after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

Mike Wood, shadow Cabinet Office minister, said: "We still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal.

"Labour did their utmost to hold this information back and it was only released because of the Conservatives humble address."

articles.title: 119 warships and counting: Kolkata-based GRSE delivers fifth submarine-hunter ‘Amini’ to Navy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In another milestone in warship-building, Kolkata-based defence PSU Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE) on Thursday delivered Amini,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In another milestone in warship-building, Kolkata-based defence PSU Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE) on Thursday delivered Amini, the fifth of the eight anti-submarine warfare shallow water craft (ASW-SWC) being built by the shipyard for the Indian Navy.Amini is the 119th warship built by GRSE and the 81st warship delivered to the Navy. Designed for operations in coastal waters, 'Amini' has the ability to undertake comprehensive sub-surface surveillance, search and attack missions, and coordinated anti-submarine warfare operations in conjunction with aircraft. Equipped with an advanced combat management system, lightweight torpedoes and anti-submarine warfare rockets, the warship is capable of detecting, tracking and engaging underwater threats, significantly enhancing the Indian Navy's capabilities to safeguard India's maritime interests and coastal waters.The ASW SWC was accepted by Rear Admiral Gautam Marwaha, VSM, CSO (Tech), Headquarters Eastern Naval Command.Measuring 77.6 metres in length, the vessel is powered by marine diesel engines coupled with waterjets, providing enhanced agility and maneuverability. With a shallow draught of 2.7 metres, the warship is ideally suited for littoral operations, enabling it to access shallow coastal waters and effectively undertake missions involving the detection and neutralisation of sub-surface threats.In keeping with GRSE’s commitment to Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Amini reflects the shipyard's strong focus on indigenous shipbuilding. The ASW-SWCs incorporate 88% indigenous content and are equipped with a 30mm naval surface gun manufactured by GRSE, further highlighting the shipyard's contribution towards developing and integrating indigenous defence technologies.GRSE is currently building 13 frontline naval platforms, comprising one Project 17A advanced stealth frigate, three ASW-SWCs, four next generation offshore patrol vessels and five next generation corvettes. In addition, the shipyard is constructing 36 other vessels, including 13 export platforms. This diverse and substantial order book reinforces GRSE's position as a key contributor to India's maritime security, indigenous defence manufacturing and growing shipbuilding capabilities.On March 30, GRSE achieved a historic milestone by delivering three frontline naval platforms — Dunagiri, Sanshodhak and Agray — to the Indian Navy on the same day.

articles.summary: RAIPUR: Tents, music, food and cars. Then came the roosters and the bets running into lakhs.
articles.body: RAIPUR: Tents, music, food and cars. Then came the roosters and the bets running into lakhs. Once a Maoist-controlled stretch of forest in Bastar, the remote terrain had acquired a different notoriety - an interstate cockfight gambling carnival attracting punters from across Chhattisgarh and neighbouring Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.Police busted the den near Raiguda village under Bhadrakali police station limits deep inside Bijapur district on Nov 3, catching 156 people and seizing more than Rs 20 lakh, 47 four-wheelers and 12 mobile phones.Acting on intelligence inputs about large-scale betting being organised under the cover of traditional cockfights, police cordoned off the forest site before moving in. articles.title: In 1984, a Texas man left 640 acres to a school district; local farmers later began working the land for free, and the harvests have now funded nearly $3 million in scholarships for about 300 students
articles.summary: In a small farming community in the Texas Panhandle, a piece of inherited farmland has become an unexpected way to help young people afford higher
articles.body: In a small farming community in the Texas Panhandle, a piece of inherited farmland has become an unexpected way to help young people afford higher education. What began with a 640-acre donation to the Gruver Independent School District in 1984 has evolved into a community-run farming initiative that generates hundreds of thousands of dollars every year for student scholarships. A November 2 report by The Washington Post, along with information from Gruver High School and West Texas A&M University, highlights how local farmers have turned their time, equipment and harvests into an investment in the next generation. The land was donated by longtime Gruver resident Karl Nielsen, who left the property to the school district. For years, the district leased it to farmers, using the rental income to support educational needs, including the purchase of textbooks and laboratory equipment. But around 15 years ago, school officials began considering whether the land could serve a much bigger purpose. During a conversation with local farmers at a high school football game, the idea emerged to use the property to fund college education directly.Instead of leasing the fields, farmers would cultivate them without charging for their labour or equipment. The crops would then be sold, with the proceeds going towards scholarships for Gruver High School students. It was an unusual arrangement that depended heavily on the willingness of an entire community to contribute. The initiative took shape around 2012, with farmers volunteering to grow corn and wheat on the district-owned property. The first students to benefit were members of the Class of 2016. Since then, the programme has distributed nearly $3 million in scholarships to approximately 300 students, according to the school district. Annual harvests generate around $400,000 for the scholarship fund, although the amount can vary depending on agricultural conditions and crop yields.How the scholarship programme worksThe Gruver Farm Scholarship Foundation was formally established on March 26, 2012. Local farmers contribute their machinery, seeds, labour and agricultural expertise, while businesses and other community members also provide support. Corn is planted in spring and wheat in autumn, with farmers regularly checking irrigation systems and managing the crops throughout the growing season.The initiative initially focused on around 410 irrigated acres of the donated property, rather than the entire 640 acres. Proceeds from selling the harvests go into the scholarship fund. A local feed yard also purchases some of the produce at above-market prices, providing an additional boost to the money available for students.The scholarship is not distributed equally among all graduates. Students build up points throughout high school based on their academic performance, test scores, participation in extracurricular activities and community service. Their accumulated points help determine how much financial assistance they receive. Individual students can receive as much as $40,000 towards their education.The programme has also evolved beyond its original purpose. An earlier account published by Texas Standard in November 2024 documented $2.5 million awarded to 277 students at that stage, while Gruver ISD's current scholarship information confirms that the initiative continues to operate.Helping first-generation graduates return homeOne of the programme's most significant outcomes has been the opportunities it has created for students whose families have never had a college graduate. According to the latest figures reported by The Washington Post, 48 scholarship recipients have become the first members of their families to graduate from college.The support has made a difference for students such as Sydney Ortiz, who graduated from Gruver High School in 2023. Her parents immigrated to the United States from Chihuahua, Mexico, and she had worried about how she would afford university. Through her academic performance, extracurricular participation and volunteer work, she earned approximately $3,000 per semester in scholarship assistance. She is now studying education at West Texas A&M University.Another beneficiary, Rhett Sparks, graduated from Gruver High in 2020 and completed an agriculture degree at West Texas A&M in 2023. The scholarship helped him avoid much of the student debt he might otherwise have accumulated. He has since returned to Gruver to work as a farmer and pesticide applicator, and plans to contribute to the farming initiative himself.Other former recipients have also returned to the area, working in professions including teaching, nursing, agriculture, mechanics and accounting. The programme has also given younger children an opportunity to understand where their future educational support comes from. Elementary school students visit the farmland during school trips, where they learn about the crops and the history of Karl Nielsen's donation.More than four decades after Nielsen left the property to the school district, his gift continues to support generations of students. What was once a source of modest rental income has become a community-funded scholarship programme, built on volunteer work and an agricultural tradition that has helped hundreds of young people pursue education without carrying the full financial burden themselves.You use AI every day. articles.title: Police car set alight in Glasgow amid Bonfire Night trouble
articles.summary: The car was torched after officers answered reports of an injured man in the Provanmill area of Glasgow.
articles.body:
A police vehicle has been set on fire and fireworks have been launched at officers as Bonfire Night disorder broke out in parts of Scotland.

Officers were called to reports of an injured man on Greenside Street in the Provanmill area of Glasgow at about 19:55 on Thursday. While in attendance, the police and ambulance crews were targeted with fireworks.

Dozens of people watched as a police car was set alight in the middle of a residential street near to other vehicles. Emergency services were forced to withdraw from the area.

Operation Amberlight specialist resources were deployed, and one man was arrested. Inquiries are ongoing and police maintain a presence in the area.

In Edinburgh, fireworks were thrown at officers in the Oxgangs area. Officers were not injured during the incident.

There was a large police presence in the area, as trouble involving groups of young people was reported.

Bonfire Night: Biggest police operation of the year under way

Police seize £12,000 of fireworks set to be sold online before Bonfire Night

Locals said groups of youths were launching fireworks at emergency services as they attempted to deal with the disorder.

Police Scotland said they received reports of youths "creating a blockage in the road" on Oxgangs Road North, Edinburgh at about 17:30.

A spokesperson said: "Officers attended and fireworks were set off in their direction, but no injuries have been reported.

"Several small fires in bins and the park were extinguished by the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service.

"Officers remain in the area, and inquiries are ongoing to trace those involved."

In Wester Hailes, the fire service attended a fire in a grass area near houses in Murrayburn Park.

Firefighters were called to the scene of a bonfire shortly after 19:00, with one fire engine called out to extinguish the flames.

Fireworks were also thrown at a fire appliance in Knightswood in Glasgow, while in Dundee, a public order unit was deployed after more than 100 youths gathered and started a fire on the road.

Reports suggest a crowd of approximately 50 people were launching fireworks and causing disorder.

A 15-year-old was taken to hospital in Alexandria after lighting a firework that exploded and damaged his eye.

Fire crews were also attacked in Castlemilk, Whitburn and Cumnock.

BBC Scotland was given access to the Strategic coordination centre at the Police HQ at Fettes.

A wall of CCTV cameras trained across Edinburgh and Glasgow flickered from empty streets to a packed Celtic stadium as officers watch for signs of disorder.

The atmosphere in the room was calm despite pockets of disorder - things seemed generally under control.

Information flashed up on screens with updates from Operation Moonbeam. As the evening progressed the screens filled up as public order units were deployed to more and more places.

Teams from Police Scotland, Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, Scottish Ambulance Service, the Scottish government and Edinburgh city council were in attendance.

Officers from as far afield as Avon and Somerset, Hampshire, Hertfordshire and South Wales were ready to be deployed.

With the additional police in place, Ch Sup David Robertson of Police Scotland said there was "evidence of improvement" but the night had still seen some challenges.

He said: "Our focus will now be on identifying individuals who haven't been identified tonight.

"Let me be clear we will do everything we can to identify them, arrest them and bring them to justice."

Chief Constable Jo Farrell issued a warning to anyone who may get caught up in disorder.

She said: "You'll face the full impact of the law, you'll be arrested and you'll face the consequences.

"I have no tolerance for that level of violence on the streets of Scotland."

She added: "I know that the planning and the work that has gone into tonight is as good as we have ever done and so we have given ourself the best, best foundation on which to ensure people can enjoy Bonfire Night."

articles.title: Government buys time on UGC rules without committing to withdrawal or retention
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Centre's move to consider a fresh review of the controversial UGC equity regulations are being seen as an olive branch to agitating upper caste
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Centre's move to consider a fresh review of the controversial UGC equity regulations are being seen as an olive branch to agitating upper caste groups, while giving BJP room to avoid a fresh caste controversy ahead of the assembly elections, particularly in Uttar Pradesh.The regulations, which extended specific protection against caste-based discrimination to OBCs alongside SCs and STs, had triggered protests among general category students who feared exclusion and possible misuse of the provisions.Centre told Supreme Court Thursday that it was contemplating setting up a committee to reconsider the regulations, ensuring that no section of students felt excluded or apprehensive. The move gives govt time to revisit the issue without committing itself to either withdrawing or retaining the rules.A complete rollback has been a key demand of upper caste organisations, whose protests also caused unease within BJP. Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh have been leading govt's outreach to agitating youth outfits. Both had met representatives of Kshatriya Karni Sena-led 'UGC Rollback Campaign' in Sept, after which a proposed mahapanchayat was postponed.The Jan notification had caused resentment among sections of general category students who felt the regulations portrayed upper castes as the principal perpetrators of caste discrimination. The absence of a specific provision against false complaints added to their concerns.At the heart of the controversy is the wording of the regulations. While one provision defines caste-based discrimination specifically as unfair treatment of SC, ST and OBC members, another prohibits discrimination against any student, including on caste grounds.General category students argue that this creates confusion over whether they would receive the same protection if they face caste-based discrimination.Supporters of the regulations argue that historically disadvantaged communities need specific safeguards against discrimination.For BJP, a complete withdrawal carries political risks. OBCs and Dalits form an important part of its social coalition, especially in Uttar Pradesh, where caste identities remain politically sensitive.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: King relishes 'politically charged' deployments, Palace aide says
articles.summary: The monarch faced questions on the UK's involvement in the slave trade during his Caribbean tour.
articles.body:
The King relishes the "tough parts" of his role and will continue to be used in "politically charged situations", a senior palace aide said at the end of the King's tour of the Caribbean.

Over the past nine days, the King visited the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda and has been used as "a great secret weapon", the aide said.

Questions over whether the UK should apologise and pay reparations for its role in the transatlantic slave trade were a theme of the visit.

"I think what we're seeing is a very clear pattern emerging of the government asking the King to head into quite politically charged situations, quite challenging situations," the aide said.

"We have to tread quite a careful line sometimes between government policy and the King's role."

The leadership of all three countries visited on the Caribbean tour wanted reparatory justice.

"I would say, in the round, this has been a complex visit. It's been challenging. It's been exhausting," the aide said. "But the takeaway is that it's been very successful and I think the King has demonstrated his statecraft both by word and deed."

Most of the King's visits outside the UK have seen him draw on some delicate diplomatic skills on behalf of his government.

In the US, he used his speech to Congress to remind President Donald Trump of the UK's value as an ally .

A year earlier he made a flying visit to Canada to welcome new Prime Minister Mark Carney as the latter faced an onslaught of threats and insults from Trump.

Visits to Germany and France in the early part of the King's reign were designed to establish new UK alliances post-Brexit.

"The King is not just King for the easy parts of the job, but the tough parts of the job, too," said the aide.

"In fact, that's probably the part of the job that he relishes most, whether that's leading on the environment, whether it's renewing and refreshing and reinvigorating relationships with nations where there have been some complex political issues at play, that is what he lives and breathes for."

The senior palace aide has worked closely with the King for many years and has a unique insight into his work and what motivates the monarch.

"He is able to reach the parts that dare I say politicians probably couldn't quite have reached," he said wryly.

The intervention of Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying he was open to the UK apologising for its role in the slave trade midway through the Caribbean tour only intensified the conversations.

The senior palace aide dismissed any suggestion that Buckingham Palace was surprised, even blindsided, by the shift in the government position saying they were told about it in a "timely manner".

English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade which saw millions of Africans enslaved and forced to work, especially on plantations in the Caribbean and the Americas.

Asked directly if the King would apologise for slavery, the senior aide laid out the chain of command in a constitutional monarchy.

"The King is the crown, the crown is the state, the state is run by an elected government, so we have to see how this whole situation plays through."

Since the start of his reign in 2022, the King has had four prime ministers - it's been a quick turnover rate with the King having to establish a new relationship each time, helped by their weekly audiences. Those close to the King view his early encounters with Burnham as a positive start.

"They get on very well. I see them together every week," explained the royal aide. "It genuinely is a good relationship, but as it is with all the prime ministers and all the ex-prime ministers as well."

Royal tours may look pretty but they can be gruelling.

There were about 40 engagements on this tour - many of them carried out in temperatures of around 35C with stifling humidity.

While the King, who is still undergoing treatment for cancer, will be 78 years old next week and the Queen will celebrate her 80th birthday next July, they are both still managing the rigours of royal visits when many of their friends are enjoying retirement.

"This is literally what he was born to do, he's very good at it, and he enjoys the reaction he gets from people in the doing of it," the aide said.

He added the King and Queen's bond after 20 years of marriage helped get them through the trickier sides of their work when things have "gone a bit wonky".

Royal tours always throw up those "wonky" moments.

In Antigua and Barbuda, at a rally to mark the country's Independence Day, a sudden downpour left the King drenched, without an umbrella and looking momentarily cross.

"You know sometimes things don't work entirely according to plan, but it was very quickly resolved, and as we saw, he was laughing… he thought it was genuinely funny," the royal aide recalled.

And in the Bahamas, the King joined dancers during a Junakanoo, a traditional carnival celebrating the culture of the islands dating back to the days of slavery.

In his speech the King spoke of the slave trade as a shameful chapter that filled his heart with sorrow as he delivered his main speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting.

He was addressing a room full of leaders where many wanted him to say sorry, offer reparations or in some cases, be removed as their head of state.

The Antiguan Prime Minister, Gaston Browne, hosted the King and Queen but wants major change including moving his country towards becoming a republic.

He said he also wanted to see "structured, inclusive dialogue on the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism".

Buckingham Palace knows the direction of travel. In 2021, Barbados removed the British sovereign as head of state. The mood was of a divorce where all parties still want to be friends… if possible. It's given neighbouring countries a taste of a something different.

"The King and the royal family are there to serve the people of these regions for as long as they wish," the senior royal aide said. "But if they don't wish it anymore, then we really are fully open to that. The family serves when it's wanted and if not, then a new arrangement can be found."

articles.title: She runs a Caribbean takeaway in England and gives free meals to people who cannot afford them; 71-year-old Florence ‘Mama Flo’ Coke has become a local hero.
articles.summary: Mahatma Gandhi very famously said, “Simplicity is the essence of Universality”.
articles.body: Mahatma Gandhi very famously said, “Simplicity is the essence of Universality”. Sometimes it is the simplest gestures that make the biggest difference in somebody's life. We come across stories of people doing extraordinary things for their community, and we too are in awe of how someone can dedicate their entire lifetime to serving others without asking for anything. What if they have understood the secret of life that most of us are still not aware of?Meet 71-year-old Florence Coke, popularly known as Mama Flo, who runs a Caribbean takeaway in Stockport, Greater Manchester, in England. While her restaurant is known for its delicious Caribbean cuisine, Florence has become equally popular for something else, i.e., making sure that no one in her community goes hungry.For more than 30 years, Florence has been living in the UK, and for the past several years, she has been running Mama Flo’s restaurant, where she has made it her mission to provide free meals to children, pensioners and people who cannot afford to pay for food. Her efforts have earned her thousands of admirers in the community, and she recently received the Pride of Britain This Morning Local Hero award in recognition of her incredible work towards making a more welcoming community.A childhood lesson that became a lifelong habitFor Florence, feeding people is not something she started doing recently. It is something she grew up watching her parents do in Jamaica. As a child, she would watch her mother prepare large pots of food every day and distribute it among the poor and the needy in her community. She saw what it meant for them and for the community and wanted to bring the same tradition to Stockport in her own way.Over the years, she has given away thousands of meals. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when the whole world was in crisis, with people losing their jobs, she continued to feed those who were struggling. As the cost of living crisis made things more difficult for families, she began providing free meals to children during the summer holidays and also sent food parcels to elderly residents who needed help. She believes that no child should have to go hungry simply because schools are closed for the holidays.'I don't like to see anyone go hungry'One particular incident that stayed with Florence was when an elderly man came to collect a free meal and thanked her for her work, explaining that he had not received his pension money and had nothing to eat. Recalling the moment, she said that she broke down and cried because it was difficult for her to imagine someone going without food.In a world where people think a hundred times before donating a cent, she is making a change in the world. Her support extends beyond the meals served at the restaurant. She works with people who deliver food to elderly residents who cannot walk up to her restaurant, while she herself spends hours preparing meals for everyone. She also tries to help people who have recently come out of prison, treating them with the same warmth and care she would offer a family member.She brings about a domino effect of change. Looking from afar, it might not look like her work is changing anything, but a little warmth of love can melt mountains. By doing such acts of kindness, she never asks for anything in return but hopes that someday they too will help someone in need.A surprise recognition for Mama FloAlthough Florence did not ask for anything in return for her work, it eventually caught the attention of the Pride of Britain organisers, who arranged a special surprise for her on ITV's This Morning. She was invited to the studio, believing that she would be appearing for a food segment, but presenters Alison Hammond and Dermot O'Leary had something else in mind. During the show, they announced that she had won the This Morning Local Hero award at the 2026 Pride of Britain Awards.Overwhelmed by the announcement, Florence said she had never expected such recognition because everything she had done over the years came from love and her desire to ensure that nobody went hungry. She also spoke about how she begins her day around 4 am, preparing food before opening her restaurant, and how she never steps out without praying.When asked about the secret behind her cooking, Florence had a simple answer: "The secret ingredient in all my meals is all love."You use AI every day. articles.title: Canada's federal budget includes billions for sovereignty and tackling homelessness
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney plans to use an oil revenue windfall to bolster Canada's economic and cultural sovereignty and address cost of living concerns.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has taken advantage of an oil revenue windfall to include tens of billions of dollars in new spending in his second federal budget, which focuses on building national sovereignty and addressing the high cost of living.

"That's what this budget does: it's the next big step in our action plan to make this country more independent, more sovereign," Carney said on Thursday.

"It focuses on growth, on people and that sovereignty, so we can live our lives as we wish."

The budget - titled Masters of Our Destiny - lays the groundwork for a Canada that is less reliant on the US for trade. It also aims to tackle the stubborn affordability crisis by promising billions to end homelessness and build new housing.

The C$142bn in new spending over the next five years is thanks to better than expected revenues from oil prices bolstered by the Iran War.

Canada's deficit is over C$50bn ($36bn; £27bn), with no path to balance.

Despite new spending, the budget shows that Carney has kept his previous fiscal goals intact.

The country still expects its GDP to grow modestly in the next year, outpacing all G7 countries except the US. Its unemployment rate, while unsteady month-to-month, is overall lower than last year.

But as people continue to feel squeezed by inflation and unaffordable housing, pressure has been building on Carney to translate his major investments into relief for the average Canadian.

And some sectors of the economy are feeling deep pain due to US President Donald Trump's tariffs on key Canadian industries, leading to thousands of job losses and uncertainty that has slowed business investment.

Here is a breakdown of some of the key takeaways for the 2026 federal budget.

A plan to end homelessness within a decade

One of the largest line items in Carney's second budget is an C$11.2bn commitment over the next four years to combat homelessness.

This includes funding for supportive housing, mental health and addictions treatment.

Statistics Canada reported last year that one in eight Canadian households have experienced a form of homelessness in their lifetime.

The government will also boost a grocery benefit that is available to low-and-modest income Canadians, which is estimated to provide C$2,570 for a family of four within one year.

Canada's opposition Conservatives have been pressing the Liberal government on cost of living, and have routinely accused the prime minister of spending too much time on foreign trade missions and not enough addressing kitchen table issues.

There are signs that Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Average hourly wages have not kept up with inflation, according to Statistics Canada. Food bank usage has hit record highs.

The average price of a home in Canada has dropped around 22% in recent years, mostly due to a clamp down on immigration. But houses are still too expensive for many in Canada's major cities - namely Toronto and Vancouver.

And like the rest of the world, the rising price of fuel has made everything - from gas to groceries - more expensive.

No boost to immigration levels any time soon

After hitting record population growth in 2023, which was fuelled largely by immigration, Canada has scaled back its newcomer targets significantly.

This includes a cap on international students and temporary foreign workers, which have been relied on by companies to ease labour shortages.

The Carney government has previously said it will keep its permanent resident admission target to 380,000 people annually until 2028.

Meanwhile, it will gradually reduce its temporary resident arrivals to 370,000.

There has been pressure on Carney to increase some of those numbers. A report from the Royal Bank of Canada in September warned that "without immigration, the country's population would shrink to half its size by the turn of the century".

On the other hand, the Conservative opposition has called on the government to further lower its targets.

In the new budget, Carney has opted to keep immigration levels flat.

Helping businesses through US tariff dispute

A big focus of the Carney government has been reducing Canada's reliance on the US as a trade partner, while also helping cushion the blow from Trump's tariffs on its key sectors.

Last year, it promised millions in backing for businesses working to develop new export markets. It also lowered Canada's marginal effective tax rate in a bid to stop businesses from moving to the US to escape tariff pains.

This budget builds on that, including plans to support specific sectors hit by US tariffs like steel and forestry.

The new funding was welcome by Canada's forestry sector, with the BC Council of Forest Industries saying in a statement that the support "comes at a critical time for workers".

Since March 2025, the Carney government has set aside nearly C$44bn in support for workers and businesses hit by US tariffs, the budget notes.

The budget states that "diversification will take time, given the scale and depth of Canada's economic relationship with the United States. But the shift is underway".

The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs

Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage

Sovereignty is a big theme in Carney's second budget, which proposes funding different measures to strengthen Canadian identity - whether it be through the arts or in space.

Canada is the only G7 country that does not have the capability to launch its own rockets. A line item in the budget looks to change that, with C$2.7bn earmarked to developing Canadian space technology and launch infrastructure.

On arts and culture, Carney is promising a tax exemption on income that is made through "original and creative artistic works".

The budget also sets aside C$32.2m over four years to establish a free national digital library for Canadians. It will launch with at least 200 titles with plans to expand in coming years.

Carney had previously pledged to significantly boost defence spending to meet the Nato target of 5% of annual GDP by 2035.

This year's budget provides some insight into where that money is being spent.

That includes a marketplace, launched earlier this year, to sell Canadian-made drones. It will get a cash injection of C$2.3bn over five years.

More funding will also go into support for Operation Reassurance, Canada's largest overseas deployment mission to deter Russian aggression in eastern Europe.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP netas accused the opposition of plotting unrest after Times Now Navbharat aired its undercover sting, "Operation Regime Change", while Congress demanded concrete evidence.BJP spokesman Gaurav Bhatia said the sting exposed alleged attempts at "regime change". He accused the opposition of preferring anarchy to democratic transfer of power. Citing alleged remarks by some of the people quoted in the sting, Bhatia warned of violent protests and Nepal-like events.Maharashtra CM Devendra Fadnavis called the matter extremely serious and said the country would function only according to the Constitution. UP deputy CM Brajesh Pathak and Union ministers Chirag Paswan, Prahlad Joshi and Giriraj Singh were among those who voiced concern.Congress RS MP Pramod Tiwari said questions should be directed at people whose statements had surfaced in the sting and concrete evidence supporting the allegations should be presented. He said Congress was in favour of a democratic transfer of power.The channel said hidden-camera conversations recorded across India raised questions about possibility of attempts to initiate regime change outside democratic process. However, it added that not all participants in conversations supported violent movements and some rejected such possibility.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Firefighter who battled COVID on front lines says he lost career for refusing vaccine: 'I'm on team Jesus'
articles.summary: Scott Carlson says he and fellow Redmond Fire Department firefighters were terminated after religious exemptions were revoked under a vaccine mandate.
articles.body: A veteran Washington state firefighter who helped respond to some of America's first COVID-19 patients says he lost the career he loved after refusing to violate his religious beliefs to comply with a vaccine mandate and is now fighting to have his day in court. Scott Carlson, a former lieutenant with the Redmond Fire Department, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that he and his colleagues spent 18 months on the front lines of the pandemic without a single case of cross-contamination before the city's vaccine requirements upended his career. "We worked 18 months with zero cross-contaminations," Carlson said. "We did our job very well. And then the governor came out and said that they wanted us to get the COVID vaccine mandate." WHO IS JAMES ERDMAN III? CIA WHISTLEBLOWER WHO WENT FROM COVID MANDATE FIGHTS TO SENATE SPOTLIGHT But when Washington officials implemented COVID-19 vaccination requirements, Carlson said he sought a religious exemption in 2021, only to learn that he would not be permitted to continue working. First Liberty Institute, which is representing eight firefighters, did not elaborate on Carlson's behalf regarding his religious exemption request. "I went through and applied for a religious exemption," Carlson recalled. "I had to prove that I was actually religious, and it wasn't just something I wanted. "And then, about 10 days later, the mayor [Angela Birney] came back and got rid of all of that and said no, and then decided to terminate all of us." According to court documents, Carlson filed a lawsuit against the City of Redmond in federal court Dec. 8, 2022, alleging that officials violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by failing to accommodate his religious beliefs and retaliating against him for requesting an exemption from the COVID-19 vaccine mandate. The lawsuit was later amended twice to include additional firefighters after they received notices from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission granting them the right to sue, according to the court filing. The firefighters are appealing a December 2025 federal district court ruling that sided with the City of Redmond, rejecting their claims that the city failed to accommodate their religious beliefs and retaliated against them for seeking exemptions from its COVID-19 vaccine mandate. Their attorney, Cliff Martin, told Fox News Digital in an interview Wednesday that the case involves more than a disagreement over vaccine policy. He alleges the city had positions available that could have accommodated the firefighters but appeared to keep those opportunities from them. OREGON SETTLES WITH CHRISTIAN MOTHER DENIED FOSTER CARE ADOPTION OVER GENDER IDENTITY BELIEFS According to First Liberty, Carlson initially received religious exemptions before those accommodations were revoked after Redmond's mayor signed an executive order. The firefighters' attorneys allege that city officials subsequently withheld information about available positions that could have allowed the employees to remain on the job. The legal team is asking the 9th Circuit to overturn a lower court ruling that rejected their claims. "We're at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, and we are hopeful that the circuit court will reverse a summary judgment order and will recognize and vindicate the victims of this religious discrimination," Martin told Fox News Digital. Martin alleged that the employer could have transferred the firefighters into other roles where vaccination was not required. "Instead, they hid those available positions from the plaintiffs and then filled them with vaccinated firefighters so that there was nowhere to transfer these unvaccinated firefighters who had a religious objection to the COVID vaccine," he said. WASHINGTON SCHOOL DISTRICT THAT FORCED KIDS TO HIDE BIBLES IN SEALED ENVELOPES MUST APOLOGIZE, PAY $275K Those allegations are central to the firefighters' legal challenge and have not been independently established in the interview material provided to Fox News Digital. For Carlson, the consequences went far beyond losing a paycheck. He said firefighting was a calling that allowed him to serve his community, use his skills and help others during some of the most difficult moments of their lives. "The emotion of losing my career, and what I feel a little bit is what my purpose is, over my faith, that was a heart divided, because I love Jesus so much that I was like, ‘Hey, I'm going to follow you no matter what. I'm on team Jesus. But dang it, this is hard.’" Carlson said the loss of his position meant losing an important part of how he served others. "This is how I serve. This is how I love on the community," he said. "So, that was a very hard emotion to say that I'm no longer going to be able to do this." Although the COVID-19 pandemic has faded from daily headlines, Carlson said the legal and personal consequences remain unresolved for people who lost their jobs during the vaccine mandate era. TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS "A lot of people say, ‘Oh, COVID's over, the pandemic's over,’ and a lot of people have varying opinions about it," Carlson said. "Most of those opinions have changed. Most people are shocked to hear that things aren't done. They hear, ‘Oh, hey, the military is having some of these cases or some of these things changed,’ or somebody else has had a success or a victory in this sense." Martin said the appeal raises fundamental questions about the extent of employers' obligations to consider religious accommodations. "No employee should have to choose between their faith and their job here," Martin said. A spokesperson for the City of Redmond told Fox News Digital that the city "does not comment on pending or ongoing litigation. The City will continue to address this matter through the appropriate legal channels."
